title: SPECviewperf 15.0.1 Linux Edition Released: Linux's Key Graphics Benchmark Adds Arm Support
gist: SPEC's SPECviewperf 15.0.1 Linux Edition adds native Arm AArch64 support for the first time, and ServeTheHome's first runs show AMD Strix Halo mini-PCs beating NVIDIA's Arm-based GB10 by 2x or more and reaching about half of a discrete Radeon AI Pro R9700. The author cautions the GB10 result may reflect immature NVIDIA Linux graphics drivers.

themes.theme: Arm AArch64 support in SPECviewperf Linux

insights.claim: SPECviewperf 15.0.1 Linux Edition is the first release of the benchmark natively available on any Arm-based system, adding AArch64 support.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Gives the industry its first standard yardstick for workstation graphics on Arm, which Arm-based mini-PCs entering the professional market have lacked.
insights.quote: marking the first time the graphics benchmark has been natively available on any Arm-based system

insights.claim: The author argues the release timing is ideal because a slate of Arm-based mini-PCs is reaching the professional market and needs a recognized workstation graphics benchmark.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A de facto benchmark arriving on Arm lowers the barrier for buyers and vendors to evaluate Arm workstation-class boxes.
insights.quote: the timing of this new release could not be better

insights.claim: SPECviewperf is described as the industry's de facto workstation graphics benchmark, so its platform coverage carries outsized weight in how hardware is judged.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Benchmark platform coverage shapes vendor marketing and purchase decisions; Arm's absence until now was a gap.
insights.quote: SPECviewperf carries an immense amount of weight within the industry

themes.theme: AMD Strix Halo vs NVIDIA GB10 in Linux graphics

insights.claim: In Linux SPECviewperf runs, both Ryzen AI Max+ 395 Strix Halo boxes outperformed the Arm-based Dell Pro Max with GB10, often by 2x or more.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD's integrated graphics currently has a clear edge over NVIDIA's GB10 in traditional workstation graphics on Linux, a point for AMD in the mini-PC segment.
insights.quote: Both Strix Halo boxes are performing far better than the GB10-based box, often by a factor of 2x or more.
insights.locator: We will start things with a focus

insights.claim: The author hedges the GB10 result: the units are configured for clustered AI workloads and NVIDIA's Linux graphics drivers have not been a major focus, so the run mainly validates that the suite works.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The GB10 gap may reflect driver immaturity rather than hardware limits, so it could narrow with driver work.
insights.quote: Take this more as a run just to validate that the Linux suite worked on the platforms
insights.locator: Our GB10 machines are set up

insights.claim: ASRock Industrial's AI BOX-A395 is called the fastest Strix Halo box the lab has tested.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Within one chip family, system-level implementation still differentiates performance.
insights.quote: remains the fastest Strix Halo box to cross our lab desks

insights.claim: Strix Halo systems typically deliver about half the performance of a Radeon AI Pro R9700 discrete card in a Threadripper 9980X system, and beat the discrete card in the NX 2406 workload.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An integrated GPU reaching roughly half of a discrete workstation card, and winning one workload, strengthens the case for compact AMD APUs in workstation roles.
insights.quote: they outperformed the discrete card in the NX 2406 workload
insights.locator: Meanwhile, to put those AMD iGPU

insights.claim: Strix Halo boxes, so far framed around AI development, are also reasonably performant for workstation graphics, provided the CPU does not become the bottleneck first.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Positions these mini-PCs as dual-use AI and CAD/graphics machines, widening their addressable market.
insights.quote: these benchmarks also show the boxes can be reasonably performant for workstation graphics tasks
insights.locator: So far, the focus on Strix Halo

themes.theme: Benchmark scope, hardware and driver limits

insights.claim: The Linux Edition covers 8 of the Windows suite's 11 benchmarks and has no DirectX, because many CAD, CAM and 3D workstation applications are OpenGL-based or not available on Linux.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Linux workstation results are only a partial view of the Windows-dominated workstation software ecosystem.

insights.claim: In practice the Linux suite supports only AMD and NVIDIA GPUs, leaving Intel out, though it does support integrated GPUs such as Strix Halo and GB10.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Intel graphics cannot be benchmarked on this standard Linux suite, a competitive handicap in workstation evaluations.
insights.quote: leaving Intel as the odd one out

insights.claim: The new snap-in architecture lets operators install only chosen workloads, which matters because a full install takes nearly 100GB.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Lower storage and setup friction should make the suite easier for vendors to adopt in routine testing.

insights.claim: ServeTheHome plans to add SPECviewperf to future GPU reviews, citing its Linux testing preference and ongoing GB10 and Radeon AI Pro R9700 coverage.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Expect more public SPECviewperf Linux numbers for Arm and AMD iGPU systems from this outlet.
insights.quote: do not be surprised if you see SPECviewperf pop up in some future reviews
